title: Recursion and Base Cases
learningObjectives: Describe the purpose of this function-related concept.
Identify its key parts or rules in an example.
Trace a simple execution or information flow.
Explain a common misuse and how to avoid it.
Apply the concept to a small programming task.

understand.concept: Recursion occurs when a function solves a problem by calling itself, often with a smaller or simpler input. A base case stops the recursive chain; a recursive step moves the problem toward that base case. Without a reachable base case or progress toward it, recursion can continue until a runtime limit or failure.
understand.whyItMatters: Recursion can express naturally nested or shrinking problems, such as traversing folders or processing tree-shaped data. Learners must recognize termination and understand that iterative alternatives may be clearer or safer for some tasks.
understand.analogy: A chain of instructions asks the next smaller question until it reaches a simple answer, then answers unwind in reverse. This is only a mental model; runtime call frames and limits matter.
understand.analogyLimit: This analogy omits language-specific implementation details; use it only as a first mental model.

explain.narrative: For a recursive function, identify the base case first, then check how each call changes the input. A trace should show the calls descending toward the stop condition and the results returning. Use recursion only when the structure benefits from it.

examples.title: Countdown
examples.code:
function countdown(n) { if (n <= 0) return; console.log(n); countdown(n - 1); }
countdown(3);
examples.explanation: The base case n <= 0 ends the calls; each recursive step decreases n.

examples.title: Factorial with a base case
examples.code:
function factorial(n) { if (n <= 1) return 1; return n * factorial(n - 1); }
console.log(factorial(4));
examples.explanation: The calls reduce to factorial(1), then multiply results while returning.

examples.title: Sum down to zero
examples.code:
function sumTo(n) { if (n === 0) return 0; return n + sumTo(n - 1); }
console.log(sumTo(4));
examples.explanation: The base result is 0; each step adds the current value.

examples.title: Trace a simple recursive result
examples.code:
function doubleDown(n) { if (n === 1) return 2; return 2 * doubleDown(n - 1); }
console.log(doubleDown(3));
examples.explanation: The return values unwind as 2, 4, then 8.

examples.title: Guard invalid input
examples.code:
function countUp(n) { if (!Number.isInteger(n) || n < 0) return 'invalid'; if (n === 0) return 0; return 1 + countUp(n - 1); }
console.log(countUp(-2));
examples.explanation: Input validation prevents an invalid negative argument from descending indefinitely.

commonMistakes: Splitting code into too many tiny pieces or overly broad components.
Ignoring inputs, outputs, or assumptions at boundaries.
Assuming runtime behavior is identical across languages.
Using abstraction or dependencies without a clear benefit.
